content: In the field of chemistry, quantitative analysis refers to the process of determining the absolute or relative abundance of one or more specific substances within a given sample. This abundance is often expressed in terms of concentration. Once the presence of certain substances in a sample is confirmed, studying their absolute or relative abundance can provide valuable insights into specific properties of the sample. For instance, quantitative analysis performed using mass spectrometry on biological samples can reveal the relative abundance ratios of specific proteins, which may serve as indicators of certain diseases, such as cancer. The term quantitative analysis is frequently contrasted with qualitative analysis. While quantitative analysis focuses on measuring the amount of a substance, qualitative analysis seeks to identify the identity or form of the substances present in a sample. For example, a chemist analyzing an unknown solid sample would first employ qualitative techniques, such as nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) or infrared (IR) spectroscopy, to identify the compounds present. Subsequently, quantitative techniques would be used to determine the precise amount of each compound in the sample. Historically, detailed procedures were developed to detect the presence of various metal ions, which are collectively referred to as qualitative inorganic analysis. Although these methods have largely been replaced by modern instrumentation, they remain foundational in the field. Similarly, tests for identifying organic compounds, often by detecting specific functional groups, are also well-established. Many analytical techniques can be adapted for either qualitative or quantitative purposes. For instance, consider an indicator solution that changes color in the presence of a specific metal ion. This solution could be used qualitatively to determine whether the metal ion is present by observing whether the color change occurs when a drop of the sample is added. Alternatively, the same indicator solution could be used quantitatively by analyzing the intensity of the color change at varying concentrations of the metal ion. This quantitative measurement would likely be performed using ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) spectroscopy.
